NVIDIA at 43 times earnings depends directly on hyperscaler budgets holding, making it far more exposed than Microsoft at 29 times if AI capex retreats.

Alphabet fell 2% and Meta dropped nearly 4% on Raedler's warning, as the chip index posted its longest losing streak since 2008.

Token prices fell roughly 50% since summer, the same monetization failure Raedler says destroyed investor returns in past booms like railroads and fiber networks.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Microsoft didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat MSFT. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

Railroads transformed America and fiber optic cable built the internet, yet many investors who funded both lost money. In a note reported on October 16, 2026, Bank of America investment strategist Sebastian Raedler argued AI is tracking the same path, writing that "most major capital cycles of the past have ended in disappointment, even though the underlying technology often lived up to expectations."

24/7 Wall St.

Raedler argues that AI's technology can succeed while investors in AI stocks still earn poor returns. Sebastian Raedler said 12-month forward consensus hyperscaler capex expectations rose from $330 billion in early 2025 to $1 trillion. Those figures forecast spending by the largest cloud operators over the next year.

The Nasdaq 100 fell 2.5%, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index posted its eighth straight loss, its longest run since 2008. After Bank of America's note, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) slid 1.43% to $214.13, a market value of $5.17 trillion. On Raedler's warning, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) fell 1.93% to $529.05, and its market value slipped below $4 trillion to $3.93 trillion.

How Capital Cycles Punish Investors

In a capital cycle, strong profits pull in a wave of investment until capacity exceeds demand. Prices then fall as competitors fight for customers, and returns on capital sink.

title: Could Shopify Stock Repeat Amazon's Run Since 2007?
detail:
Could Shopify Stock Repeat Amazon's Run Since 2007?
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 12:17 AM CDT 5 min read
SHOP
AMZN
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors who bought Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) stock at the end of 2007 have watched their shares climb over 50-fold since then. It's natural to ask what e-commerce company could do something similar next.

With its stock near a record, Shopify (NASDAQ:SHOP) is a clear candidate. Shares of the e-commerce software company closed at a record $179.22 earlier this week, and they trade around $170 as I write.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

And on size alone, the comparison works surprisingly well. Shopify's revenue for the last 12 months was about $13.3 billion. Amazon's revenue in 2007 was $14.8 billion.

But Shopify isn't built the way Amazon was, and its stock isn't valued the way Amazon's was in 2007. For anybody buying shares today, I think the second difference matters most.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Shopify is growing like Amazon did

Amazon's 2007 was a strong year. Its revenue climbed 39%, and its free cash flow, or the cash Amazon had left after paying for capital spending, more than doubled to $1.18 billion, crossing $1 billion for the first time.

Shopify's growth looks similar, and it's been accelerating. Showing how much faster merchants are selling through the platform, Shopify's gross merchandise volume (GMV, the total value of orders placed through Shopify) grew 20% in 2023, 24% in 2024, and 29% in 2025. It's also cleared 30% year over year in each of the last four quarters. In the second quarter of 2026, GMV rose 32% year over year to around $116 billion, after 35% growth in the first quarter, and revenue climbed 34%.

Shopify's already ahead on cash. Its free cash flow for the last 12 months came to around $2.4 billion, up about 29% from the year-ago period -- and about twice Amazon's 2007 number, on a bit less revenue. That's a free cash flow margin of around 18%, against about 8% for Amazon in 2007.

Put another way, judged by free cash flow, Shopify's business arguably looks stronger now than Amazon's did at the same size.

Not a retailer

This cash gap comes from a core difference between the two companies. Amazon in 2007 was mainly a retailer. Products sold by outside sellers were just 28% of the units sold on its sites that year, so most of its revenue was the full price of goods Amazon sold itself.

Shopify doesn't sell the products. Its merchants do. Shopify charges them for its software, and its merchant solutions business, which brings in around three-quarters of revenue, earns most of its money from processing their payments.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock trades at 78.2 times sales, compared to 3.1 for the S&P 500. Investors paying that premium need to know exactly what they are buying, and the case Palantir makes has evolved. During the fiscal Q3 2024 earnings call, executives highlighted the fast-growing number of U.S. businesses signing on as customers. By the latest call in fiscal Q2 2026, the focus had shifted. So what does management talk up now?

Palantir Now Makes The Case For Sovereign AI

By sovereign AI, Palantir means an architecture where companies maintain full control over their own data and the artificial intelligence built upon it. During the fiscal Q2 2026 call, held August 3, 2026, executives reported immense demand from enterprises for this capability. They contrasted this approach with purchasing external services from AI labs, a process they described as paying outside vendors to move proprietary corporate knowledge into third-party models.

The pitch sounded quite different during the fiscal Q3 2024 call. At that time, leadership highlighted that Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count grew to 321. Expanding that baseline served as a clear signal that more U.S. companies were adopting the software.

While Palantir still reports the customer count, the metric no longer takes center stage. Instead, the company links sovereign AI directly to increased spending per client. Customers that previously utilized only the Foundry software now want access to the broader sovereign AI stack. The core argument now rests on the size of individual customer commitments, rather than the sheer number of clients.

Shifts like this test every retirement plan. If your advisor recently retired, it is a good moment for a free second opinion from our partner firm.

Palantir's Business Customers Are Spending Much Larger Sums

Sales to the U.S. businesses are growing much faster than the number of businesses buying. Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count reached 653 in fiscal Q2 2026, up 35% from a year earlier. Over that same period, U.S. commercial revenue rose 149% to $764 million. These buyers belong to Palantir's commercial segment, a division that generated $2.07 billion in fiscal 2025, accounting for 46.3% of the company's total revenue that year.

Contract values follow a similar trajectory. U.S. businesses signed deals with Palantir worth $2.132 billion in total in fiscal Q2 2026, up 153% from a year earlier. Consequently, the average customer is committing significantly more capital than they were just a year ago. Executives labeled that contract total a record, forming the foundation of the case they now present.

Investors holding Trade Desk (TTD) have seen the stock lose 74.1% of its value over the past year, compared with a 17.9% return for the S&P 500. The immediate question is how much further shares might drop. One certainty is the current level: at $13.13 on October 15, the stock sits above the prices where it turned and rallied three times in 2018. How did the stock fare at this price then, and how has it fared in 2026?

How Trade Desk Stock Has Fared At This Price

In the past, shares climbed significantly from these levels. Rallies started between $11.61 and $12.57 in August, October and December 2018. All three advanced to the same high of $27.86 in July 2019, delivering a gain of 139.6% for the typical run.

More recent tests of this price played out differently. Over the two years ending October 15, 2026, the stock returned to this level twice, hitting it on August 10 and September 22, 2026. Both times, it fell 5% before it rose 20%. Following the second instance, shares closed at $11.92 on October 6. They then recovered to the current price with a 7.8% rise on October 15. The bounces that define this price support are eight years old.

Questions like this one test every retirement plan. If your advisor recently retired, it is a good moment for a free second opinion from our partner firm.

What You Could Make If Trade Desk Reaches Resistance

Resistance sits at $19.56, marking the price where a rally stalled once in the past two years. If the stock reached that level, $10,000 invested today would be worth about $14,900. By comparison, the typical 2018 bounce would have turned that same sum into about $23,960. A climb to current resistance represents a smaller move than those earlier rallies. On the way up, the stock would need to pass $15.09, another price where a prior rally stalled once.

Investors are currently paying little for those profits. Shares trade at 15.1 times the last twelve months of earnings, compared with 22.7 for the S&P 500. During the same call, management indicated that most of the top 100 accounts were still growing by double digits from a year earlier. They also noted that Audience Unlimited, a product moving to open beta, was showing very encouraging results.

Walmart (WMT) stock trades at 42.5 times earnings. Among the six retailers in its peer group, only Costco Wholesale is priced higher. Walmart ranks lower on business performance than on price. Over the latest four fiscal quarters, Walmart sits third out of six on revenue growth and fourth on operating margin. So how does Walmart's price look beside the rival that grows fastest?

Walmart Trades At Twice Amazon's P/E With Slower Growth

Amazon.com is the fastest grower in the group. It trades at 20.2 times earnings. Net income exceeded operating income at Amazon, meaning items outside its operations added to the earnings behind that P/E. Amazon revenue rose 15.8% over its latest four fiscal quarters, compared with 6.2% at Walmart. Amazon also posted an operating margin of 12.1%, well above the 4.4% at Walmart. Amazon is a broadline retailer, and Walmart is a consumer staples merchant. The two margins come from different kinds of business.

Costco operates in Walmart's own industry. It is priced higher at 47.1 times earnings. Costco's revenue also grew faster than Walmart's, rising 10.1%. Target and Home Depot are priced below Walmart and grew more slowly. Walmart maintains a price near the top of the group, while its growth sits in the middle and its margin sits in the lower half.

What Are You Buying At Walmart's Price?

Investors buying Walmart at this price are mostly buying its home market. The Walmart U.S. segment brought in $486 billion of the company's $713 billion revenue in fiscal 2026. The retailer sells at such high volume that a small change in margin represents a lot of money. In fiscal Q2 2027, with sales of $188 billion, each percentage point of margin is worth about $1.9 billion of operating profit.

Walmart is finding its faster growth in businesses built around those sales. The global advertising business grew 38% in fiscal Q2 2027. Walmart's membership fee revenue rose 17%. Management said almost half of Walmart's profit growth came from areas such as membership, advertising and marketplace, a trend the company expects to continue. The current share price appears to assume Walmart keeps growing these businesses fast enough to lift its margin.

(0:15) - Should You Consider Investing Into The Magnificent 7?

(32:00) - Episode Roundup: AMZN, TSLA, AAPL

Podcast@Zacks.com

Welcome to Episode #457 of the Value Investor Podcast.

Every week, Tracey Ryniec, the editor of Zacks Value Investor portfolio, shares some of her top value investing tips and stock picks.

She has talked about the Magnificent 7 stocks (aka, the "Mag 7" stocks) many times over the years. While they are considered growth stocks, occasionally, there are some which look like values.

There have been buying opportunities for value investors in the past.

In March 2024, Tracey encouraged Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway to buy Alphabet given its free cash flow and low valuation with a forward P/E of just 17. Alas, he didn't listen to her until 2025, but better late than never.

Should value investors be looking at any of the Mag 7 stocks right now?

Who is cheap and who is not?

The Cheapest and the Most Expensive Mag 7 Stocks Right Now

1. Tesla, Inc. (TSLA)

Tesla is not the cheapest of the Mag 7 stocks. It's the most expensive, on a price-to-earnings (P/E) basis. It trades with a forward P/E of 215 but was at 225 at the time of the recording of the podcast.

Shares of Tesla have fallen further in the last few trading sessions. It's now down 22% year-to-date, which makes it the worst performing Mag 7 stock this year.

Earnings are expected to rise just 1.2% this year but rebound another 33.9% in 2027.

Tesla is now a Zacks Rank #4 (Sell) stock ahead of its earnings report on Oct 21, 2026.

Should both value and growth investors stay away from Tesla with these valuations?

2. Apple Inc. (AAPL)

Apple is still the largest equity position in Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio. But Berkshire Hathaway bought Apple a decade ago when its P/E was under 10. Apple now trades with a forward P/E of 36. That is a historically high valuation.

Earnings are expected to rise 18.8% this year but only 7.7% in 2027.

Apple also trades with a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 10.7. A P/S ratio over 10 is a high valuation, even for a growth stock. Apple is an expensive stock.

Shares of Apple are up 26% year-to-date to new all-time highs. It's the best performing stock in the Mag 7 this year.

Is it risky for value investors to buy Apple right now?

3. Amazon.com, Inc. (AMZN)

Shares of Amazon are up only 8% year-to-date. That is underperforming the S&P 500 which is up 11.8%.

Earnings are expected to rise 81.6% in 2026 and another 18.7% in 2027. With that kind of earnings growth, but with the shares not going anywhere, it shouldn't be a surprise that Amazon has a forward P/E of just 19.6. This is historically the lowest Amazon has traded at on a P/E basis.
